description: Held-out Memories for collecting fresh Smart Robot traces. Written for this eval, not player data, not in Training or GS-T6.

memories.text: On the slow train to my grandmother's village I pressed my face to the window and counted water buffalo. My father bought peanuts in a paper cone at every station. The seats were green vinyl and stuck to my legs. When we arrived it was already dark and the platform smelled of rain.

My uncle held the back of my bicycle seat and ran beside me down the lane. I did not know he had let go until I turned and saw him far behind, waving. I fell into the hedge a moment later. I still have a small scar on my elbow from that evening.

The morning of my final exam the power went out, so I studied by candlelight at the kitchen table. My mother made tea without saying a word and left it by my elbow. I walked to school early and the streets were empty and quiet. I passed, but I remember the tea more than the questions.

Every summer the fruit seller at the corner market saved the ripest mangoes for my sister. He wrapped them in newspaper and refused to take the full price. We ate them on the steps outside with juice running down our wrists. The year he retired the corner felt smaller.

The only time it snowed in our town, school closed and nobody knew what to do. My brother and I built a lopsided snowman with a carrot nose and a scarf from the cupboard. By afternoon it had melted into a gray heap on the grass. We took one blurry photo that my mother still keeps.

Our dog slipped out of the gate during a thunderstorm and we searched the streets until midnight. My father called her name in a voice I had never heard him use. She came back on her own at dawn, muddy and shaking, and slept on my feet all day. After that we fixed the latch.

My grandfather listened to cricket on a small radio with a cracked case. He would lean close and turn the volume up whenever the crowd roared. I did not understand the rules, but I learned to cheer when he cheered. The radio still sits on his shelf, silent now.

At the beach I found a shell shaped like a spiral staircase and carried it home in my pocket. It broke on the bus, and I cried more than I expected to. My aunt glued the pieces together that night under a lamp. The crack runs right through the middle, and I like it better that way.

My first night in the college hostel I could not sleep because of the ceiling fan's clicking. My roommate offered me half of his biscuits and told me about his home in the hills. We talked until the birds started outside. He is still the friend I call first.

During the festival we lined the balcony with clay lamps and tried to keep them lit against the wind. My little cousin kept relighting the same stubborn one. Fireworks burst over the rooftops and the smoke made our eyes water. Later we sat on the floor and shared sweets from a steel box.

The day I got my first library card I borrowed the maximum of five books and could barely carry them. The librarian stamped each one with a date and smiled at my stack. I read all five in a week, mostly under the blanket with a torch. I returned them early just to borrow five more.

We flew kites from the flat roof every winter afternoon, and the sky filled with color. My kite tangled with the neighbor's and both strings snapped at once. We watched them drift away together over the water tank. He laughed so hard that I could not stay angry.
